title: Why The Blue Tsunami Rattled AI Stocks - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Stock Market Suffers Damaging Weekly Losses The trillion-dollar AI data center boom will likely face even greater scrutiny after Democrats won control over Congress and governors' mansions in several key states. The results have shaken AI stocks, highlighted by the past week's volatile trading. The Nasdaq tumbled sharply Thursday, before bouncing back Friday. Top AI stocks are set to close the week lower while the cloud giants also had a wild ride, with volatile trading for Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL).  The action underscores the challenges ahead for the AI megatrend after a Blue Tsunami election. Backlash to data centers — which act as the engines powering AI technology — has led to calls for moratoriums, bans and other legislation. The results in Texas were particularly striking. Ed Mills, the Washington D.C. policy analyst for Raymond James, said what happened in the Lone Star state, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, could prove most impactful for AI stocks. Risk Management: How Invested In The Market Should You Be Right Now? "To use a different storm analogy, this is arguably a category five hurricane that hit the data center trade," Mills told Investor's Business Daily. "You have a candidate that has won, who said that the old moratorium was a scam and that, if elected, she would put in place a real moratorium. Now that's just Texas, but you also have a similar thing in Ohio." Hinojosa made opposition to data centers a key part of her winning campaign for Texas governor. She called for a broader moratorium on data centers until new legislation is passed. She was critical of a freeze Abbott placed on permits earlier this year. Additionally, she argues he would lift it following the election. Texas trails only Virginia for total data centers active or in the works, according to estimates from Pew Research. It is also the site of massive data center efforts such as the Abilene Stargate campus. Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia also made data centers a campaign issue. Following the midterms, research firm Cleanview found 41% of the current U.S. data center pipeline is located in states that have a governor or governor-elect pledging restrictions on the facilities. Data center backlash will bring challenges to Amazon, Microsoft and Google. The tech giants are the three leading cloud-computing providers. Each so-called cloud hyperscaler is spending hundreds of billions to build new data centers to meet demand. But the stock reactions following the midterms point to a more nuanced picture. Amazon, Microsoft and Google actually rallied on Wednesday. Then they pulled back sharply with the rest of the AI trade Thursday. On the one hand, restrictions on new data centers likely provide an edge to the biggest, most established cloud computing providers. Hyperscalers are the AI incumbents, as Needham analyst Laura Martin wrote to clients following the midterms. "We believe higher regulatory barriers entrench incumbents, and increase risks (and raise required ROICs) for new entrants," Martin wrote, referring to return on invested capital. Investors may not be all that upset if AI spending is forced to slow. Soaring capital costs have eaten the free-cash-flow of even tech's biggest players, raising concern on Wall Street in the lead-up to the elections. Some tech investors will view the midterms as a "slight positive" if the results force Big Tech to "hit the slow down button" on capital spending, Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote on Wednesday. At the same time, AI demand has helped accelerate revenue growth for each of the three leading cloud businesses. Restrictions on data centers risk either raising costs or making it more difficult to meet demand. Meta Platforms (META) President Dina Powell McCormick said at a Wall Street Journal conference on Wednesday that building data centers in the U.S. is "going to be harder" following the midterm results. Tech companies may look to international markets, she added. While it doesn't operate an enterprise cloud infrastructure business, Meta is spending hundreds of billions on data centers to support its AI ambitions and massive portfolio of social media apps. The midterms fallout was also pronounced for companies that provide components used for the AI buildout, from chips and computer hardware to energy and construction. Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell sharply Thursday, its worst day since it tumbled after the release of Chinese AI model DeepSeek in January 2025. Nvidia also bounced back Friday, but was on track for a weekly loss. Other leading AI players also had a volatile week. Shares of Seagate (STX), Dell (DELL), Micron (MU) and CoreWeave (CRWV) were also poised to end the week in the red. Analysts with UBS estimate that data center pauses or moratoriums could put about 30% of the capacity previous expected in 2028 at risk. "The slowdown is a negative for Semis and AI infrastructure, but a lot is already priced into semis with valuations nearing multiyear lows," UBS strategist Keith Parker wrote in a client research note Wednesday. SpaceX (SPCX) is also a major developer of cloud infrastructure and AI.  Shares fell 4% Wednesday and 9% Thursday before regaining some ground Friday. Investors are also likely bracing for blowback from Elon Musk's big donations to Republican politicians. Investors are likely still sizing up the broader impact for AI stocks. Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani said in a client note that increased scarcity could drive up prices for AI compute. Amazon, Google and Microsoft are poised to close the week higher. Amazon offered a bullish signal Wednesday by breaking a recent downward trendline drawn from a record high reached on Aug. 3. That was followed by a pullback Thursday and slight gain Friday. Microsoft jumped up from a test of its 50-day moving average Wednesday before easing back by 3.5% Thursday. Microsoft is the top-rated among the hyperscaler stocks with a best-possible 99 IBD Composite Rating, according to IBD Stock Checkup. The score combines five separate proprietary ratings into one rating. The best growth stocks have a Composite Rating of 90 or better. Google stock is still trading near recent lows that followed its Q3 earnings, despite the gains Wednesday. Nvidia is sharply below its 200-day moving average with the postelection tumble. Meanwhile, Raymond James' Mills said the backlash to data centers is tied to factors that extend well beyond the structures themselves. They have also come to represent concerns about AI's impact on jobs and even national security. "In a lot of these conversations, you see as much as 75% of the American people opposed to data centers," Mills said. "And it's not just because of affordability. It's not just because of environmental issues. It is the physical manifestation related to a lot of anxieties all wrapped up into one." That could make both data centers and AI fertile ground for politicians to run against in future elections. In the comments of that post, I emphasized a clear warning: all it would take is a single external catalyst to slow down hyperscaler demand, and the cycle would turn rapidly. This structural vulnerability wasn't limited to hardware commodities. On October 23, in my post "Inside the Neocloud Trap: What CoreWeave $CRWV , Nebius $NBIS , and the AI Gold Rush Are Hiding," I exposed another high-risk subsector: Neoclouds. I detailed how Hyperscalers (Amazon $AMZN, Alphabet $GOOG, Meta $META, Microsoft $MSFT) were merely renting external compute capacity from players like CoreWeave and Nebius as a temporary buffer while their own data centers were under construction. I warned that these Neoclouds—trapped in high-yield junk debt (10%-15%) and deeply negative Free Cash Flow—would face a severe liquidity squeeze the moment Hyperscalers completed their internal capacity or slowed down external demand. Many retail investors were in total denial, as the comment sections of those posts clearly show. With that context established, let’s look at what actually triggered yesterday’s steep market crash. Beyond the Headlines: The Electoral Trigger Behind the Market Panic To understand what actually triggered yesterday’s panic, we have to look at the results of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections. While midterm elections naturally command market attention, the primary driver behind this specific sell-off wasn't just party leadership shifts—it was the underlying voter sentiment that swept candidates into office. Across key battleground states like Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, the debate over AI infrastructure took center stage. Democratic victories—most notably Gina Hinojosa defeating Greg Abbott in Texas on a platform advocating for strict moratoria and legislative oversight on data centers—were largely powered by a widespread voter backlash against energy consumption. The core message that resonated with voters was straightforward: local communities and everyday taxpayers are absorbing the inflated energy costs and grid constraints generated by massive AI compute facilities. The exit poll data from the Associated Press and The Wall Street Journal (analyzed by Amrith Ramkumar) illustrates the central role this issue played at the ballot box: As the chart demonstrates, over 55% of Democratic voters cited opposition to unbridled data center expansion and its impact on household utility bills as a "Crucial" (23%) or "Major factor" (33%) in their voting decisions. This political shift introduces immediate regulatory friction, potential permitting delays, and higher energy overhead for future physical infrastructure buildouts. It is critical to put this electoral shift into operational context. In my view, this is not going to completely stop data center construction in the United States—the underlying structural demand for compute is far too massive. However, it forces big tech hyperscalers and infrastructure developers to pull up a chair to the negotiating table with local Democratic administrations and utility regulators. This creates a brand-new layer of regulatory friction, permitting delays, and energy tariff reviews that will inevitably slow down the overall growth rate of data center buildouts for the foreseeable future. To quantify exactly where this slowdown will hit hardest, we only need to look at the current U.S. capacity pipeline: As clearly illustrated in the chart, the regulatory threat doesn't jeopardize capacity that is already Operational or Under Construction. The core bottleneck hits the massive wall of projects sitting in the Early Stage (green) and Committed (blue) phases. In key states carrying the largest pipelines—such as Texas (63 GW), Georgia (42 GW), and Virginia (41 GW)—the political requirement to audit grid impact and review utility rate structures means many of these mega-projects will face extended delays before receiving final approval. Future compute capacity won't disappear, but it will come online at a significantly slower pace than what the market had priced in for hardware and memory suppliers. title: The AI infrastructure boom faces a "global crackdown": restrictions on construction are crossing the Atlantic, with Microsoft's (MSFT.US) Amsterdam project at the eye of the storm. - 富途牛牛
content: The wave of restrictions on AI data center construction, triggered by the U.S. midterm elections, is spreading across the Atlantic to Europe. The wave of restrictions on AI data center construction triggered by the U.S. midterm elections is spreading across the Atlantic to Europe. Zhitong Finance APP has learned that on Friday local time, a group of protesters broke into a Microsoft (MSFT.US) data center construction site in Amsterdam, kicking off a two-day rally. This is part of a growing global backlash against the rapid expansion of computing power required for AI. According to the "Stop Dirty Data Centres" coalition, activist groups have announced actions in 16 countries on Friday and Saturday. The coalition brings together environmental organizations and digital rights movements to jointly call for a moratorium on large-scale construction. Reportedly, over 100 activists gathered at a Microsoft AI data center construction site in Amsterdam on Friday. They marched arm-in-arm, then breached the site, climbed construction cranes, hung balloons, and danced inside while police monitored from the sidelines. Some demonstrators held signs reading: "Tear down your data centers." The site owner, Pure Data Centres, plans to invest over $1 billion, with backing from Oaktree Capital, a subsidiary of Brookfield. The company stated it is committed to engaging with local stakeholders. "We urge those on-site to evacuate safely and engage in dialogue with us regarding this project and the concerns raised," the company said. Other planned protests include marches in Dublin, demonstrations outside the parliament building in Warsaw, and another protest targeting a Microsoft data center in Denmark. Microsoft stated that it understands the strong public opinions surrounding the project and respects the right to peaceful expression, but does not support any illegal activities. Tech stocks face sell-off amid market concerns over tightening AI regulation From Spain to India and the United States, resistance is gaining momentum. Driven by market fears that Democratic control of Congress could lead to stricter regulations stifling the AI boom, U.S. tech stocks fell sharply on Thursday. Senator Bernie Sanders' earlier proposal for a "national moratorium on new data centers," combined with the explicit commitment by the governor-elect of Texas—one of the most important hubs for AI data centers in the U.S.—to pause approvals for new projects, jointly triggered this "reckoning-style" sell-off across the AI supply chain. Protesters argue that data centers exacerbate strains on electricity and water resources, compete with housing and other industries for scarce resources, and hinder the achievement of climate goals. They also highlight risks of job losses, the concentration of computing power in the hands of large tech companies, and potential threats to personal and national security. Tech companies responded that data centers are the core infrastructure for meeting global demand for AI and cloud computing, serving as critical facilities for enterprises, governments, and general consumers. The “Stop Dirty Data Centres” coalition emphasized that it does not oppose technological progress nor call for the shutdown of existing data centers; rather, it advocates pausing new large-scale projects until clear regulatory frameworks are established in respective countries. In response, Europe faces internal contradictions: on one hand, it seeks to catch up with AI development in the United States and Asia to boost productivity; on the other, it aims to maintain relatively strict regulatory and public protection mechanisms. Henna Virkkunen, the EU’s top digital official, stated in an interview on Thursday that Europe needs more data centers to support AI development, but construction must proceed prudently. “AI is undoubtedly a crucial technology, and we must possess sovereign computing capabilities.” Virkkunen noted that Europe is ramping up chip manufacturing and investment in AI startups, with plans to establish a number of large-scale computing facilities within the region. However, she added, “For the public, one point is crucial: people must be assured that electricity bills will not skyrocket due to data centers, that power outages will not be triggered by computing infrastructure, and that such projects must not harm the environment.” It is reported that Google’s (GOOGL.US) project in Finland has been subject to a criminal investigation over land-clearing issues; Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental regulations for data centers; and Microsoft previously withdrew from a data center project in the UK due to delays in infrastructure development. title: What Are Microsoft Investors Betting On? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Microsoft (MSFT) stock trades at 26.8 times its adjusted earnings over the last twelve months. This profit figure leaves out one-time items and adds back stock-based pay after tax. That is a lot to pay for a single year of profit, and the multiple is about the same, 26.7 times, against the profit analysts expect for fiscal 2027. That forecast may not add back stock-based pay, so it may count profit on a different basis. The stock only looks cheaper against fiscal 2028 profit. So what kind of growth are you paying for at today’s price? The consensus forecast projects Microsoft’s revenue rising about 19% in fiscal 2027, to $395 billion. For fiscal 2028, the forecast anticipates sales growth of 20.5% and net income growth of 20.9%. The forecast’s net margin is 37.7% in fiscal 2027 and 37.8% in fiscal 2028. This means the profit growth you are betting on comes from more sales, not from wider margins. Based on the consensus forecast, Microsoft stock trades at 26.7 times fiscal 2027 earnings and 22.1 times fiscal 2028 earnings. Its trailing multiple on adjusted earnings is 26.8 times. Has Microsoft Delivered Sales Growth Near The Forecast? For fiscal 2027, Microsoft is close. Revenue grew 18.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, and management guided for growth of 18% to 19% in fiscal Q2. Over the last twelve months, though, revenue grew 17.9%. This means the fiscal 2028 forecast expects faster sales growth than Microsoft has delivered. That growth is uneven across the business. In fiscal 2026, Microsoft’s Intelligent Cloud segment grew 29.7%, while its More Personal Computing segment shrank 1.1%. Microsoft reported a net margin of 40.3% in fiscal 2026. The consensus forecast has a lower margin in both coming years. The forecast does not specify whether its profit is reported or adjusted, meaning the two margins may not be measured the same way. The likeliest place is data center capacity. On its October 28 call, management said customer demand continues to exceed available supply, and some third-party GPU capacity Microsoft was counting on for fiscal Q2 has moved into the second half of the fiscal year. Management guided for Azure growth of 49% to 50% in fiscal Q2 and said Microsoft needs further efficiency gains across its fleet to reach it. Any further delay would leave Microsoft less to sell and pull the sales forecast down. Microsoft has worked around these delays once already: Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, ahead of management’s expectations, even with third-party capacity arriving late. Price is the other place the forecast could slip. Management said the price Microsoft gets per token, a unit of AI work, can change through the quarter. Foundry, its platform for building AI agents, more than tripled its revenue from a year earlier in fiscal Q1 2027. Management named higher revenue per token as one reason Foundry beat expectations. A fall in that price would pull the sales forecast down too. If Microsoft delivers the consensus forecast, the multiples on fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 earnings are a fair picture of what you pay for the stock. If capacity arrives late or token prices slip, profit could fall short of the forecast. Those multiples would then understate what you pay, making the stock a riskier bet. Azure growth against management’s guide is the number to watch, and Microsoft is expected to report it in January 2027. Forecasts can slip, and so can markets. title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Compounds Nscale's IPO Troubles By Walking Away From Texas Data Center Expansion - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 5, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis Nscale’s path to a public listing is narrowing as Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) declines to exercise an option that would have more than doubled their existing computing agreement at a Texas data center. Reuters reported Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the decision was made several months ago, predating Nscale’s IPO filing in September. Microsoft’s existing workflow under the original contract remains intact, and the Texas pullback does not alter the terms of the deal already in force. The two companies signed an agreement in 2025 for Nscale to deploy roughly 200,000 Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) AI chips across its data centers in both Europe and the United States. The Texas decision is the second significant retreat by Microsoft from Nscale commitments, following its exit last month from a deal to anchor Nscale’s flagship Essex, UK data center project. Power connection delays at the Essex site pushed the expected supply date into the 2030s, prompting Microsoft to walk away from that anchor arrangement entirely. Nscale, which counts Nvidia among its backers, is already under pressure from investors who have pushed back on its $130 billion IPO valuation target, according to a report published last month. The broader cloud sector is adding to the anxiety, with debt-laden neocloud operators such as CoreWeave drawing increased scrutiny amid persistent concerns about overcapacity across the industry. Political headwinds are also emerging, as the Democrats’ decisive midterm victory introduces the prospect of stricter AI regulation that could make new data center construction harder and more expensive. Separately, delays tied to IREN Ltd (NASDAQ: IREN) were cited by The Information as a factor in Microsoft spending less than it had budgeted for capital expenditures in its most recent quarter. Retail traders on Stocktwits have turned negative on the stock, with sentiment flipping to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish,’ and one trader captured the market’s mood bluntly: “$MSFT microsoft jumped 6% today on a bet the build slows down. seems like the best ai news left is less ai spending, and a rally for not building tells you where the capex story actually stands.” Despite the turbulence, MSFT shares remain up 15.6% year to date through their last closing price, reflecting how broader market enthusiasm for AI has so far outweighed concerns about infrastructure execution. title: US Futures Mixed After Rally On Wednesday — MU, TSLA, AAPL, MSFT, APP, NVDA, IREN In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. equity futures were mixed early on Thursday after the previous session's rally, helped by a sharp drop in oil prices and greater clarity following Democrats’ midterm victories. As of 3.45 a.m. ET, S&P 500 futures fell 0.11%, while Nasdaq-100 futures declined around 1%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures moved in the opposite direction, gaining 0.5%. The cautious start followed a strong session on Wednesday, when major U.S. indexes closed higher as technology and semiconductor stocks rebounded. The S&P 500 ended 2% higher on Wednesday, while the Nasdaq-100 advanced 1%. The Dow climbed 3% to its highest level in a year. The small-cap Russell 2000 also added 1.6%. Oil prices rebounded in early Thursday trading after initially extending their losses, as investors weighed whether Republicans’ setbacks in this week's congressional elections could lower the risk of further escalation in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Brent crude futures rose around 1.05% to $95.61 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 0.3% to $88.38 as of 3:45 a.m. ET. The recovery followed a sharp sell-off on Wednesday, when both benchmarks plunged more than 8% to settle at their lowest levels since August 31. Micron Technology (MU): Micron came under pressure in early premarket trading on Thursday, with shares down over 3% as concerns about tighter AI regulation compounded weakness across technology stocks. Democratic Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona called on Wednesday for a pause in advanced AI development until adequate regulations are in place. The prospect of stricter rules has raised concerns that congressional action could slow data center expansion and limit demand for AI computing capacity. Tesla (TSLA): A potential Tesla-SpaceX merger is facing fresh questions as political pressure on Elon Musk adds to concerns about regulatory hurdles and the value of any takeover premium. Mark Tepper, CEO of Strategic Wealth Partners, raised doubts about the prospects of such a deal, stating that greater scrutiny of Musk could create challenges for both companies. His comments followed Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress and the Texas governor's race. Texas is home to major Tesla and SpaceX operations, as well as their planned Terafab chipmaking project. Tesla shares had dropped 3% on Wednesday, taking their weekly losses to nearly 4%, and were down 2.2% in early premarket trading on Thursday. Apple (AAPL): Apple crossed the $5-trillion valuation mark on Wednesday as its shares climbed to a 52-week high, supported by optimism around its earnings outlook and stronger device demand. Investors have also responded positively to expectations of improving cost conditions and the company's upbeat revenue forecast. The stock gave up some ground in early premarket trading on Thursday, slipping 0.15% at the time of writing. Microsoft (MSFT): Microsoft's latest earnings and continued growth in its Azure cloud business helped drive the stock to a 52-week high on Wednesday. Adding to the optimism, Bill Ackman's Pershing Square said in its third-quarter investor letter that Microsoft is well-positioned to benefit from growing AI adoption through Azure, Copilot, and GitHub. The stock was up 0.08% in early premarket trading on Thursday. AppLovin (APP): The stock was among the biggest premarket gainers on Thursday after the advertising technology company reported record third-quarter results on Wednesday. Revenue jumped 55% year over year, while net income rose 72%. The stock had already gained 10% during Wednesday's regular session and climbed around 18% in Thursday’s premarket trading. Nvidia (NVDA): Nvidia faced renewed pressure as concerns over tighter AI regulations and possible delays in data center projects weighed on semiconductor stocks. The prospect of stricter rules under the incoming political landscape has raised questions about the pace of AI infrastructure spending. Investors are also debating the sustainability of the sector's rapid expansion, including concerns over circular financing and off-balance-sheet debt used to fund large AI hardware purchases. Nvidia shares were down around 1% in early premarket trading on Thursday. IREN (IREN): The stock remained on traders' radar after coming under heavy selling pressure on Wednesday, with shares plunging 11.4% during the regular session. The decline came as cloud and AI stocks faced pressure following Democrats' midterm victory. The company also faced scrutiny after a report linked its business to Microsoft's lower AI capital spending in the previous quarter. Then falling share prices will make it harder for the companies to borrow, tightening the dollar liquidity crypto depends on, Hayes wrote. "This presents an issue for the general market environment because the entire AI trade rests on vibes. Hayes compared the setup to Zcash (ZEC) back in 2016. The stock can only be supported with an increase in free cash flow, Hayes said. He also said Musk would have to return that cash through dividends or buybacks. title: Microsoft Stock Has Gained More Than 50% in About 4 Months. Here's What It Has Usually Done Next. - The Motley Fool
content: The software giant has run this fast 13 times before. How did the following year usually go? Microsoft (MSFT -0.99%) shares jumped nearly 7% on Wednesday, Nov. 4, as U.S. stocks rallied the day after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections. The stock sits near $553 as of this writing. That leaves it about 57% over its June 25 close of $352.83, and the rise took just 92 trading days. A move like that is rare for a company worth about $4 trillion. But Microsoft has done it before. Going back through its daily closing prices to 1986, I find 13 past runs like this one. In 11 of them, the stock was up a year later, with a median one-year gain of around 33%. It's a solid record. But it might mean less than it seems. Microsoft stock has climbed in around 74% of all one-year periods since 1986, fast run or not. And the latest run, in July 2025, is one of the two that finished down. Every run starts the first day Microsoft closed at least 50% over its lowest close in the past 92 trading days. I used split-adjusted prices without dividends, and runs had to begin at least one year apart. "A year later" is the close 12 months after a run started (or the last trading day before it). By this rule, the current run began on Oct. 6. Ten of the 13 past runs came between 1986 and 2001, when Microsoft was a much smaller company. The biggest years came in that stretch, too. Shares more than doubled over the year after the runs that began in November 1986, January 1991, and March 1998. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,360,613 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The one early miss followed a January 1988 run, when the stock was recovering from the October 1987 crash, and shares were around 12% down a year later. Since the 2001 run, Microsoft has only moved this fast three times. The stock gained around 12% over the year after June 2009 and about 33% after June 2020. Then it lost about 13% after July 2025. Even some of the good years were rough. After the January 1992 and January 2001 runs, shares slid over 20% at one point before ending the year higher. Microsoft's latest fast run hit the 50% mark the day after its fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter report on July 30, 2025. The July 31 close of $533.50 was around 50% over the April 8 low. Investors paid about 38 times earnings then, using the $14.13 a share Microsoft earned in fiscal 2025 on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis. Shares drifted mostly sideways over a few months. Then they fell all the way to that $352.83 close on June 25, 2026 -- around 34% below where the run began. Even a 15% gain the day after Microsoft's fiscal 2026 report in late July didn't erase the loss, and on July 31, 2026, shares were still about 13% down from a year earlier. I'd say the starting price mattered more than the pace of the run. At around 38 times earnings, the shares could fall a long way on any hint of trouble. In a couple of ways, I think it is. Adjusted earnings per share grew 22% in fiscal 2026, and the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended Sept. 30, 2026) added another 18% gain, to $4.89. For the past four reported quarters, adjusted earnings were about $18.04 a share. At roughly $553, the stock costs about 31 times adjusted earnings, well under the 38 times earnings investors paid in July 2025. Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing platform, is also accelerating. Its revenue climbed 40% year over year in the quarter that ended September 2025, then 42% in the quarter that ended this June and 48% in the last one. Of course, that growth takes a lot of money. Microsoft's cash from operations rose 29% from a year ago. But free cash flow dropped about 27% to $18.6 billion as the company poured more cash into data centers. What has Microsoft stock usually done after a run like this? It has usually kept rising. But that record only modestly beats the stock's odds in any given year, and the most recent case went the other way. The business looks stronger than it did in July 2025, and the stock is cheaper relative to its earnings. Still, with free cash flow shrinking, paying about 31 times adjusted earnings just after a 57% run isn't something I'm eager to do. title: Election Results And Falling Oil Prices Fuel Broad Market Rally As Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) And Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Flash Buy Signals - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 5, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis, Politics A twin catalyst of election outcomes and sharply lower crude oil prices drove a powerful postelection stock market surge on Wednesday, lifting equities across a wide range of sectors. The Dow Jones Industrial Average led the charge with a gain of 3.03%, signaling strong investor confidence in the post-election economic outlook as capital rotated aggressively into blue-chip names. Oil futures told a parallel story, with the benchmark crude contract declining 0.94%, easing cost pressures for businesses and consumers alike and adding further fuel to the broader rally. While the headline indexes surged, the picture inside the technology sector was more complicated, with many tech stocks retreating even as select mega-cap names broke sharply higher. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) posted a gain of 5.15%, with the stock flashing a clear buy signal that caught the attention of traders looking to position ahead of further postelection momentum. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) outpaced even Apple’s move, climbing 5.66% and triggering its own buy signal, reinforcing the view that institutional money was selectively rotating into the largest and most liquid technology names. Amazon also joined the group of stocks generating buy signals during the session, adding a third mega-cap name to what analysts described as a meaningful cluster of technical breakouts. Meta Platforms offered a more muted performance, gaining just 0.38%, underscoring the uneven nature of the rally even within the top tier of the technology universe. Stocks across many non-technology sectors were among the session’s clearest winners, with buy signals emerging broadly as investors responded to the combination of political clarity and lower energy costs. Market watchers cautioned, however, that at least one sector was best avoided despite the overall bullish tone, suggesting that not every corner of the market was positioned to benefit equally from the postelection environment. The divergence between the surging Dow and the mixed performance within tech highlights a broader rotation that investors will need to navigate carefully as the post-election landscape takes shape in the days ahead. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

Here’s a roundup of key earnings and non-earnings news from the ongoing week: Shares of chipmakers, neocloud operators and key AI infrastructure firms fell on Wednesday and extended their slide in overnight trading as Democrats, who support AI regulations, won in both the House and Senate. AMD reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and forecast fourth-quarter sales above Wall Street estimates, and also said it expects sales to grow 80% in 2027, buoyed by demand for data center chips. The report came after Intel’s tepid forecast last week, which pressured the company's shares and the broader sector. Notably, AMD forecast December-quarter sales above Intel’s outlook. If both companies meet those targets, AMD would outsell Intel for the first time in their history. Apple, Inc. (AAPL) shares tumbled after it said gross profit margin will continue to fall due to surging memory chip prices, which it expects to keep rising well into next year. The messaging shifted focus from an otherwise upbeat fiscal fourth-quarter report, the first under new CEO John Ternus, with total and iPhone sales beating analyst expectations. The companies said the combination would create a leader in connectivity for artificial intelligence data centers by joining Marvell’s chips and electrical connections with Lumentum’s lasers and optical parts, which move data using light. Meta announced a $15-billion bond sale to help pay for its expanding AI infrastructure. On Wednesday, Democrats captured both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats, 24 House districts, five governorships, and twelve state legislative chambers, securing an early reported majority of at least 231–141 in the House and 54–44 in the Senate. After an initial dip, markets reversed green on the blue tidal wave. According to The Kobeissi Letter, U.S. stocks added more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization in their first day of trading after the midterms. The relief rally spilled over to the bond markets as well, with the 10-year Treasury yield falling below the 5% threshold to around 4.90%, back in what Yardeni Research called the "old normal" range of 4% to 5%. However, markets were concerned that a potential slowdown in the massive artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout was on the horizon with the Democrats at the helm. Experts are divided on how the midterm election results will affect the AI rally that has been building for the better part of three years. Yorkville Advisors partner and managing director Dan Ives said in a post on X, “Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years. Will slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…some investors will like the “slower pace”…others view it as adding risk. We estimate 10% of datacenters will not happen now.” However, Yardeni Research said in a post on Wednesday that even if the Democrats slow the AI buildout, profits and free cash flow for hyperscalers will ultimately increase and “fewer AI-related bond issues would also help keep a lid on bond yields.” In recent months, a flood of bond issuances from AI hyperscalers has pushed corporate borrowing rates higher, pressuring bond markets and stoking concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade. According to a Reuters report, technology-related debt issuance in the U.S. has surged more than $250 billion so far this year, up 81% from the ​same period last year. However, Fundstrat’s Tom Lee said in an interview with CNBC that Democratic gains in the midterms could prove positive for stocks and dismissed the selloff in data-center and AI-related names as a short-term reaction. He said the AI trade remains intact, noting that rising compute demand as more users adopt AI tools would likely lead many states to still welcome the investment, even if on stricter terms. James E. Thorne, Chief Market Strategist at Wellington Altus, said that the blue wave would likely lead to a shift in the “doomer narrative,” adding that it was wrong to assume that America won’t build data centers, and that the AI trade is over. “For the record. Slowing Data Centre build out and stopping the Iran war will be good for bringing inflation down,” he said in a post on X. Carson Group’s Ryan Detrick also doubled down on his bullish thesis for the AI trade, saying in an episode of ‘The Glass Half Full’ that despite recent volatility, the “AI wave is real” and that “this is an economy that's going to surprise to the upside. We still think this bull market's alive and well.” Beyond the AI slowdown, markets are also anticipating legislative gridlock, as Democrats will likely seek to challenge Trump's policy agenda, raising the risk of debt-ceiling standoffs and government shutdowns. “Beyond the occasional deal on must-pass legislation, the next two years will likely be characterized by gridlock, with the White House increasingly focused on foreign policy while Democrats concentrate on ‘messaging bills’ and investigations in order to set the narrative ahead of the 2028 presidential elections,” Morningstar DBRS analysts led by Michael Heydt, senior vice president, sector lead, global sovereign ratings, reportedly said. “However, an inter-branch standoff could set the stage for government shutdowns and brinksmanship over the debt ceiling … the outgoing Republican-led Congress will need to pass another [continuing resolution] to fund the government until the incoming Democratic-led Congress is sworn in on January 3, 2027, or run the risk of a government shutdown. The debt ceiling will also need to be raised in 2027. We expect the executive and legislative branches will reach an agreement to raise the debt ceiling in a timely manner. However, failure to lift the debt ceiling would have adverse implications for the economy and could, if the Treasury materially delays non-debt payments, result in a downgrade of the US credit rating,” they added. AMC Entertainment Holdings (AMC) stock is heading for its best weekly gain since July, after the theater chain posted record third-quarter (Q3) revenue and Adjusted EBITDA, and CEO Adam Aron declared on X that AMC “has recovered”—a stock attempting to claw back four years of losses. AMC Entertainment stock traded over 2% lower overnight, ahead of Thursday. The stock has gained 15% so far this week and is on track to reverse four years of losses. The rally tests whether a record quarter can change how Wall Street prices a company that spent years as a survival story. AMC still reported a nine-month GAAP net loss, and its stock trades at a valuation unlike its peers’. Aron is betting that a $10 billion-plus box office makes the old debt and dilution worries obsolete. For the better part of four years, AMC Entertainment’s story was about staying alive. This week, its CEO argued that story is over. “Today, we can finally say that AMC has recovered,” Aron posted on X after the company reported Q3 results on Wednesday. He called the quarter “a triumph” and said AMC’s biggest and best in its 106-year history. The numbers back him on growth. Q3 revenue rose 31.6% year-on-year to $1.711 billion, up from $1.300 billion last year. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 183.7% to $347.5 million, nearly triple last year’s figure. Adjusted EBITDA margin hit a record 20.3%, more than double the 9.4% from a year ago. It was the second straight quarter in which AMC set all-time company records for both revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Analysts had expected about $1.62 billion in revenue and earnings of $0.10 a share, according to Fiscal.ai estimates cited by Stocktwits. AMC reported adjusted earnings of $0.13, against a loss of 58 cents a year ago. Operating cash flow was $176.6 million, versus a $14.9 million outflow a year ago. Free cash flow was $109.3 million, which brings the year-to-date total to $124.7 million. That is why Aron sees AMC posting positive free cash flow for all of 2026. Cash and equivalents more than doubled to $751.9 million, excluding $39.6 million in restricted cash. Attendance did the heavy lifting. Q3 attendance rose 28.3% to 74.9 million moviegoers, with international markets up 41.5% and U.S. markets up 23.3%. AMC did this with slightly fewer screens, averaging 9,177 versus 9,354 a year ago. The company also reported record revenue per patron, which Aron credited to its loyalty programs and its growing roster of premium large-format auditoriums. Aron also leaned on the balance sheet. On Oct. 5, AMC completed a $3.97 billion refinancing covering about 97% of its debt, pushing maturities out to late 2031 and 2033. During the Q3 earnings call, Aron addressed critics directly. He called any future article describing AMC as overly debt-laden “mindlessly in error.” He said “groundless fears of endless share dilution will come only from those looking in the rearview mirror.” He did not rule out new stock sales, saying AMC will “wisely utilize equity financings when it makes sense.” His argument rests on the macro backdrop. AMC now operates in a box office above $10 billion, he said, “a very different animal” from the $7 billion to $9 billion range of the past four years. Q4 looks strong so far. Aron said October’s domestic box office ran about 35% above the same month last year. The remaining slate includes The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday and Jumanji: Open World. He expects the domestic and global box office to reach their highest full-year levels in seven years. AMC has gained about 125% in 2026 as of late October, ahead of IMAX (IMAX), Cinemark (CNK) and streaming giant Netflix (NFLX). Even with record quarters, its first nine months produced a net loss of $19.2 million, or $0.03 share. Nine-month adjusted net earnings were a modest $26.9 million. Until GAAP profits become consistent, valuation arguments for AMC will rest on EBITDA and cash flow rather than earnings. The next few months will decide whether this week’s 15% gain is the start of a re-rating. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory the previous day. The stock has registered a 192% increase in message volume over the past week. Another user said, “$109.3 million in quarterly free cash flow with expectation for positive free cash flow for all of 2026! Stay Zen AMC family. Our time will come.” AMC stock has gained 40% in the past twelve months. Read Next: Why Did AAPL, MSFT, AMC Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs? title: MSFT Stock Surges Above $555 to New Record Highs as Midterms Lift Microsoft and Big Tech - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock has rallied above $555 to a new record after recovering from a decline toward $500, as strong cloud growth and improving sentiment following the U.S. midterm elections support buyers, despite growing scrutiny of infrastructure spending and future computing commitments. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have staged a sharp recovery after falling toward $500, with the stock extending its gains today to break above $557 and establish a new record high. The rebound follows renewed concerns about the company’s relationship with Anthropic, rising infrastructure costs and the substantial investment required to expand its computing capacity. Improving sentiment across technology stocks following the U.S. midterm elections has provided another catalyst. Investors are reassessing the potential impact of political pressure on data-centre construction, particularly as electricity costs, grid stability and water consumption become increasingly important issues. Greater regulatory scrutiny could force hyperscalers to reconsider the pace of infrastructure expansion. Although this could create operational challenges, investors may also view more disciplined spending as positive for free cash flow, which has become a major concern across the technology sector. The removal of election uncertainty has also allowed markets to refocus on corporate earnings, economic conditions and the outlook for large technology companies. However, the implications of the election results for tariffs, fiscal negotiations and government policy remain uncertain. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results demonstrated continued strength across its core operations. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue increased to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while earnings comfortably exceeded the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Despite the strong performance, the market reaction highlighted a growing distinction between earnings growth and the returns generated from infrastructure investment. Investors are increasingly questioning whether Microsoft’s spending commitments can translate into sustainable profitability and sufficient cash generation. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. The performance highlights continued demand for cloud computing services and Microsoft’s ability to attract enterprise customers. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. CEO Satya Nadella also highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, expanding cloud capacity requires substantial investment in data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors. The challenge is ensuring that revenue growth keeps pace with capital expenditure rather than allowing infrastructure costs to weaken margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone, revering lower. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments to Microsoft through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. The disclosure relates to an existing arrangement amended during 2026 and highlights the scale of future computing demand. However, large commitments do not eliminate the risks associated with financing and infrastructure expansion. Smaller cloud providers could face greater pressure if borrowing costs remain elevated or customer demand fails to meet expectations. Recent warnings from Elon Musk about the sustainability of some infrastructure businesses have added to concerns about debt-funded data-centre construction. Microsoft has a stronger financial position than many smaller competitors, but it still needs to demonstrate that these commitments will generate attractive returns. Microsoft is also investing in its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver significantly higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and improve infrastructure efficiency. However, development, deployment and scaling require substantial investment before those benefits become fully visible. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the status of those discussions remains unclear. Not every division is experiencing the same momentum. Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%. Regulatory pressure also remains a consideration. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace could add further pressure as businesses reassess subscription costs and available alternatives. The move above $557 marks a significant recovery from the recent decline toward $500. Strong earnings, 30% Microsoft Cloud growth and substantial future computing demand continue to support the company’s fundamentals. However, the central question remains whether Microsoft’s infrastructure commitments and custom-chip investments can deliver sufficient returns. The latest rally suggests buyers are regaining confidence, but elevated spending, financing risks and regulatory scrutiny remain important considerations as the stock enters record territory.

Bernstein noted that, for major vendors such as Oracle and Microsoft, the downside risk of OpenAI's computing power commitments is low. Zhitong Finance APP learned that as the AI lab has signed contracts to use a significant portion of the under-construction AI computing capacity, market concerns about customer concentration risk continue to mount. In this report, Bernstein uses OpenAI's annual contract commitments as a proxy for all AI labs and arrives at a conclusion contrary to the panic narrative: although the commitment scale is large, it is tiered over time and not entirely irrevocable; as capacity and related costs grow, so do OpenAI's leverage and payment capabilities—meaning that for major suppliers such as Oracle (ORCL.US) and Microsoft (MSFT.US), downside risk is low. Bernstein maintains an "Outperform" rating on Microsoft and Oracle (with price targets of $722 and $325, respectively) and an "Underperform" rating on CoreWeave (with a price target of $54): It has no concerns about its existing backlog but doubts its ability to renew contracts and secure additional deals with strong economics. Bernstein first clarifies the narrative: the media claim that "OpenAI has committed over $1.5 trillion" reflects a long-term vision rather than a specific contract. Two more reliable data points are as follows: in October 2025, OpenAI stated that Stargate had secured nearly 7 GW of planned capacity, with investments exceeding $400 billion over the next three years, and had already locked in commitments for $500 billion and 10 GW by the end of 2025; a July 2026 report, meanwhile, estimated OpenAI's cloud-computing infrastructure spending through 2030 at approximately $750 billion. Bernstein's bottom-up model estimates that, assuming all contracts are delivered on time—which the report explicitly calls "highly unlikely"—OpenAI's infrastructure spending through 2030 would total approximately $614 billion; on an annual basis, the peak of currently committed spending occurs in 2031 at about $184 billion. Signing a $750 billion contract does not equate to paying out $750 billion in cash before 2030 for three reasons: First, chips from NVIDIA, Broadcom, and AMD will likely be financed by suppliers and paid for over roughly six years based on the hardware's lifespan, with delivery schedules and quantities remaining uncertain; second, agreements with AMD and Cerebras include warrants that vest in tiers tied to AMD's stock price, meaning these chips could effectively cost OpenAI little or nothing depending on share-price movements; third, the self-built Project Camellia data-center shell—roughly $20 billion, 3.2 gigawatts in Georgia, phased into operation from 2028 to 2032—is a long-lived asset that could have been capitalized over time or financed differently, but the report treats it as a front-loaded expense. Key demand-side data: According to the report, OpenAI told investors that its annualized revenue at the end of September was close to $50 billion, with total revenue up 77% year over year. Extrapolating from this, OpenAI's revenue next year would exceed $80 billion, surpassing the report's estimate for infrastructure spending in 2027 (excluding the $15 billion Camellia supercomputer). The report projects that OpenAI's infrastructure spending will grow about 58% year over year in 2028 to $139 billion (or $129 billion excluding the supercomputer). As long as revenue growth remains at or above 60%, revenue is expected to continue outpacing infrastructure spending. Bernstein notes that OpenAI has consistently exceeded its revenue targets in every reporting period; at the industry level, global annual inference spending ultimately needs to reach five to twenty times training spending, and we are still in the early stages. Oracle's relationship with OpenAI centers on a $300 billion deal, comprising multiple tranches of 5- to 6-year capacity contracts (signed in 2025, effective from 2026, rolling out through 2030, with Bernstein expecting the bulk to occur in 2028). Bernstein estimates Oracle can recognize approximately $312 billion in revenue, with 57% booked before its fiscal year 2030; OpenAI accounts for less than 50% of Oracle's RPO, and this share will continue to decline as other businesses grow. Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI is complex: as an investor, model user, and capacity supplier, Microsoft previously announced that OpenAI has contracted to purchase an additional $250 billion in Azure services, with each tranche structured as a 6-year contract aligned with hardware lifecycles. Amazon has two agreements: a $38 billion, 7-year deal signed in 2025, and a $100 billion, 8-year agreement signed in 2026 as part of their collaboration (including up to 2 GW of Trainium chips). CoreWeave (CRWV.US) has contracts with OpenAI totaling approximately $22.4 billion ($11.9 billion signed in March 2025 along with a $350 million equity investment, $4 billion in May, and up to $6.5 billion in September), but Bernstein emphasizes that the contract language specifies "caps" rather than committed revenue. Although Google (GOOGL.US) has been repeatedly rumored to have capacity and TPU agreements with OpenAI, it lacks contractual evidence verifiable in financial reports, leading Bernstein to exclude it from the model. The report specifically cites two canceled cases: OpenAI had reached an agreement with Oracle to expand the Abilene 2.1 GW project in Texas, but later withdrew and ceded the adjacent 900 MW site to Microsoft/Crusoe; the developer Crusoe found a replacement tenant within about two weeks. Similarly, after OpenAI pulled out of the Stargate project in Norway (a collaboration between Nscale and Aker) announced in July, Microsoft took over. These examples illustrate a significant gap between "announcements" and "irrevocable contracts." Bernstein judges that AI labs are pushing ahead with capacity far exceeding actual needs, and a normalization of supply and demand may occur within the next two to three years. The real risk to the industry lies not in the scale of commitments made by leading labs, but in speculative construction and low-quality business models spurred by the easing of capacity scarcity. Bernstein reiterated its skepticism about neocloud's business model, believing that labs will increasingly rely on hyperscale cloud partnerships, hosting agreements, and self-built infrastructure. (AMC) stocks surged to 52-week highs on Wednesday as a Democratic midterm election sweep and earnings momentum lifted Wall Street sentiment. Apple crossed a $5-trillion valuation, while Microsoft's stronger-than-expected earnings and 48% Azure growth fueled gains. Apple and Microsoft stocks gained 5% and 6%, respectively, while AMC Entertainment stock climbed 7%. Apple stock reached an all-time high of $354.5, taking the iPhone maker's market capitalization beyond $5 trillion. Investors responded to expectations of stronger device demand, improving cost conditions, and the company's upbeat revenue outlook. Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management said in an X post that slower capital spending on data centers across the technology industry could reduce pressure on memory component prices, potentially supporting Apple's future profitability. The company's December-quarter revenue forecast calls for 7% to 10% growth, ahead of Wall Street's 6% estimate. Bernstein also increased its Apple price target to $380 from $370, citing better-than-anticipated quarterly performance and encouraging revenue guidance for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Meanwhile, Apple introduced the initial developer versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The software includes new artificial intelligence capabilities for Series 12 and Ultra 4 watches, including Siri Recap. However, on Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘bearish’. Microsoft stock also reached a record high of $559.15 on momentum from the company’s stronger-than-expected fiscal first-quarter 2027 results. Revenue increased 19% year-on-year to $92.28 billion, exceeding analyst expectations of $90.62 billion. Earnings reached $4.92 per share, comfortably ahead of the $4.71 consensus estimate. Its cloud business remained a major growth engine. Azure revenue climbed 48% to $33.17 billion, beating expectations of about 45% growth. Commercial remaining performance obligations, which represent contracted business yet to be recognized as revenue, increased 73% to $677 billion. Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square, in its Q3 letter, said that Microsoft is well positioned to profit from AI through Azure, Copilot and GitHub. The investment firm added that rising enterprise adoption, flexible pricing and expanding AI services could accelerate growth and strengthen customer relationships. XTB research director Kathleen Brooks also warned that increased congressional scrutiny could delay a transaction. “While Congress cannot stop a merger, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny,” she said. Gary Black, managing partner of The Future Fund, warned that an all-stock SpaceX-Tesla deal might deliver less value than bulls expect, pointing to Marvell Technology’s (MRVL) acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE). “As we’ve learned (again) from $MRVL - $LITE deal, a +24% premium can quickly go negative as the acquirer’s stock is sold down,” he said on X. Marvell’s initial offer promised 4.5 shares for each Lumentum share, worth about $1,132, a 24% premium to Lumentum’s Oct. 28 closing price. But the fixed exchange ratio means the offer’s dollar value falls alongside Marvell’s stock. With the deal expected to close in the first half of 2028, Black warned that Tesla investors could face a similarly lengthy wait. “A SPCX-TSLA deal given its size and complexity could take just as long,” he said earlier this week. Calacanis, who is also an All-In podcast co-host, praised Uber’s latest quarterly results and named it a top pick alongside Tesla. The call follows his $1 million in purchases of each stock last month. “Demand, growth, free cash flow and a strong position in the emerging AVs market make this my number one pick alongside $tsla right now,” he said on X. He expects ride-sharing’s share of rides to rise from about 1% to 30% within his lifetime, creating opportunities for both companies. Calacanis predicted both stocks would triple in under five years, calling them as “50% undervalued.” His latest forecast follows a separate bet on autonomous vehicle takeovers. In September, Calacanis disclosed small positions in WeRide (WRD), Pony.ai (PONY), Lucid (LCID) and Rivian (RIVN), predicting that all four would be acquired within 24 months. “Consolidation is coming to the autonomous space based on the massive progress that Tesla, Waymo, and Uber are making,” he said at the time. “I believe these four companies are going to be bought in the next 24 months and I expect, as a group, that I will 2x my investment in under two years.” He called those smaller positions as investments with a one-to-four-year horizon, compared with his usual intention to hold equities for more than a decade. Calacanis backed his bullish bet with sizable purchases. Late last month, he disclosed buying 15,000 Uber shares at $65 for $975,000 and 3,000 Tesla shares at $357 for about $1.07 million. His 12-month targets favored Uber: $120 implied 85% upside from his entry price, while Tesla’s $500 target pointed to about 40%. A $189,000 Netflix (NFLX) purchase brought the three trades to $2.24 million. Calacanis also sees room for both Uber and Tesla in autonomous driving. Free cash flow reached $2.54 billion for the quarter and a record $10.4 billion over the preceding 12 months. Growth still faced hurdles. It plans to launch a driverless Nuro-Lucid service in the Bay Area in early 2027, followed by supervised Rivian deployments in 2028 before moving to fully driverless operations. Meanwhile, Tesla is advancing its own service. The company said Cybercab rides began in Austin on September 3, with its robotaxi fleet reaching nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the third quarter. He expects these core holdings to deliver returns several times those of the index over the next decade. He also holds about 10 smaller speculative positions, which he would cut if their products and business fundamentals stopped improving. content: Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT) announced that Emma N. Her experience and engagement contributed to the success of the company on a broad range of issues throughout her board service. Microsoft (Nasdaq “MSFT” @microsoft) creates platforms and tools powered by AI to deliver innovative solutions that meet the evolving needs of our customers.  started its new fiscal year with a quarter that exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. The result reinforced its position as one of the most closely watched names in US Technology Stocks, with cloud and artificial intelligence services once again doing most of the work. The headline figure was Azure, the company's cloud platform, which grew even faster than in the prior quarter. Management said demand continues to exceed available capacity, a message that suggests the AI build-out has further to run. Azure is now Microsoft's single biggest business line, a remarkable shift for a company once defined by Windows and Office. Growth accelerated on demand for AI training and inference workloads, along with steady migration of traditional enterprise applications to the cloud. The broader Microsoft Cloud division also accelerated. Management described a fast start to the fiscal year and pointed to customers committing to larger, longer contracts. Commercial productivity cloud revenue continued to grow steadily, helped by the rollout of AI assistants across productivity software. The commercial remaining performance obligation, a measure of contracted revenue not yet recognised, surged to a record. This backlog provides unusual visibility and shows that customers are locking in cloud and AI capacity for years ahead rather than paying for short-term needs. Microsoft reorganised its reporting into an Agents and Infra unit, which captures much of the cloud and AI business, and a Devices and Consumer unit. The infrastructure side grew strongly, while devices and consumer revenue slipped, reflecting softer demand for Windows hardware and gaming. The new structure makes the company's priorities clear. Most incremental revenue and profit now comes from cloud infrastructure and AI agents sold to enterprises, while consumer products play a supporting role. To meet demand, Microsoft continues to invest heavily in data centers, chips and networking. Capital expenditures roughly doubled from a year earlier, and management signalled a large spending plan for the full fiscal year. Unlike some peers, Microsoft's operating cash flow still comfortably covers this investment. Reported profit was also boosted by gains linked to its investment in a leading AI model developer, which widened the gap between reported and adjusted growth. Investors generally focus on adjusted figures for a cleaner view of underlying performance. Guidance pointed to continued strong growth in the coming quarter, with Azure expected to grow at a similar or slightly faster pace in constant currency. Management again said capacity constraints remain, meaning revenue growth is partly limited by how quickly new data centers come online. That is an unusual position for a company of Microsoft's scale. It implies demand is not the bottleneck; supply is. As new facilities open, the company expects to convert more of its backlog into revenue. The scale of investment is the main concern. If AI demand slows, or pricing for AI services falls faster than expected, returns on new data centers may disappoint. Power availability, chip supply and regulatory scrutiny of large technology platforms are further factors to monitor. Competition is also intensifying. Rival cloud platforms reported strong growth this season, and custom chips from cloud providers are changing the economics of AI infrastructure. Microsoft's broad enterprise relationships remain a powerful advantage, but no platform has the market to itself. Beyond infrastructure, Microsoft is pushing AI agents into everyday business software. Tools that draft documents, summarise meetings and automate routine tasks are being bundled into enterprise subscriptions, giving the company new ways to raise revenue per user. Adoption across large organisations is still building, but management sees it as a long-term growth layer on top of the cloud. Developer tools and security products also benefit from AI features, strengthening the overall ecosystem and making it harder for customers to switch providers once their workflows are built around Microsoft platforms. The partnership with a leading AI model developer remains a significant strategic asset. It gives Microsoft early access to advanced models for its cloud and software products, while the developer relies on Azure capacity for training and serving its systems, deepening ties between the two organisations. As a heavyweight in the Nasdaq Composite, Microsoft's results help set the tone for the entire technology sector. This quarter offered reassurance that enterprise demand for cloud and AI services remains robust, even as markets debate the overall size of AI spending. The next reports are likely to focus on how quickly capacity expands, whether Azure growth stays near current levels and how AI assistants translate into broader software revenue. For now, the company enters its fiscal year with clear momentum. Microsoft Corporation MSFT emphasized accelerating cloud demand, infrastructure efficiency and expanding AI monetization during its first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call. Management highlighted strong Azure growth despite capacity constraints and increasing investments in AI infrastructure. CEO Satya Nadella outlined Microsoft's strategy to integrate Copilot, Foundry and Azure into a unified AI platform. CFO Amy Hood emphasized operational efficiency and disciplined resource allocation as the company scales capacity to meet demand. Microsoft reported first-quarter adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share, exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.71. Revenues increased 19% year over year to $92.28 billion, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $90.58 billion. Microsoft Corporation Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Microsoft Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Microsoft Corporation Quote Operating income increased 21%, while operating margin reached 50%, supported by revenue growth and platform efficiencies. Hood attributed the results to stronger cloud demand, improved infrastructure utilization and disciplined operating expenses, which increased 6% year over year. Microsoft Cloud revenues reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year. Azure revenues grew 48%, exceeding management's expectations despite delays in third-party capacity deliveries. Hood highlighted Foundry revenues more than tripling, benefiting from GPU efficiency gains and higher revenue per token. During the analyst Q&A, a UBS analyst questioned Azure's growth drivers. Hood explained that infrastructure efficiencies and improved CPU monetization helped Microsoft serve additional demand without equivalent capacity additions. For the fiscal second quarter, Microsoft expects revenues between $96 billion and $97.1 billion, representing 18% to 19% year-over-year growth. Hood projected Azure revenue growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency, supported by continued infrastructure efficiencies. Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud revenues are expected to grow approximately 19% in constant currency. Management cautioned that customer demand continues to exceed available supply. Delayed third-party GPU capacity deliveries, shifting into the fiscal second half, remain an operational constraint. Capital expenditures totaled $45.2 billion during the quarter, with approximately three-fourths allocated to short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. Hood expects fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion, bringing projected calendar-year spending to approximately $170 billion. During the Q&A, a Bank of America analyst questioned Microsoft's financing strategy. Hood highlighted leasing arrangements, potential debt financing and continued positive free cash flow as sources of financial flexibility. Nadella highlighted accelerating enterprise Copilot adoption, with daily users increasing nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year over year. Customers deploying more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased more than eightfold year over year. Meanwhile, customers actively consuming Copilot credits through usage-based billing grew more than 75% sequentially. A Stifel analyst questioned consumption monetization beyond software development. Nadella acknowledged that adoption outside coding would progress more slowly, while Hood emphasized investments in specialized customer-facing teams and revised sales processes. Devices and Consumer revenues declined 3% to $15.5 billion, reflecting challenges across Windows and gaming. Windows OEM and devices revenues decreased 22%, while Xbox revenues declined 2%. Hood cited weaker PC demand, elevated inventories and difficult comparisons following Windows 10's end-of-support cycle. For the fiscal second quarter, management expects Devices and Consumer revenues between $15.9 billion and $16.4 billion, with Windows OEM and devices revenues declining in the mid-30% range. Nadella emphasized that Microsoft's integrated AI infrastructure enables workloads to be allocated across different products according to demand and economic returns. Hood reiterated that revenue growth, platform efficiency and focused operating investments remain central to sustaining profitability while expanding AI capacity.  announced on Monday that they are widening their working relationship so that the companies can jointly pitch network connectivity for artificial intelligence workloads to large business customers. AI systems are only as useful as the data they can reach. Large organisations typically keep information in several public clouds, in private data centres, in branch offices and in partner environments, and the links between those places were often built a project at a time. The announcement describes that patchwork as fragmented and complex, and treats it as a brake on AI deployment. Lumen said it plans to make its cloud networking and application connectivity suite available through Microsoft's cloud and AI ecosystem. The company's pitch rests on network scale and control that customers can switch on as needed, which contrasts with the older model of ordering a fixed circuit and waiting for installation. Alkira provides software that orchestrates connections across clouds, sites and data centres, and, combined with Lumen's network, gives enterprises a single portal to connect, secure and manage hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Katy Brown, a corporate vice president for Americas markets and industries at Microsoft, said the company is committed to giving customers choice as they connect existing environments to Azure. title: Texas Goes Blue: What Gina Hinojosa's Win Means For AI Data Centers And Stocks Like MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, CRWV - Stocktwits
content: In a major shakeup, Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, toppling one of the nation’s most prominent Republican governors and supporters of President Donald Trump, Greg Abbott. Dem. James Talarico won the state’s Senate seat, defeating Rep. Ken Paxton. The elections are significant as Hinojosa is seen to be critical of the breakneck buildout of AI data centers, a key part of the AI boom that is bringing billions of dollars in sales for chip, infrastructure and software companies. In July, Hinojosa called for a temporary Texas-wide pause on new data centers until lawmakers pass protections. Her proposals include requiring data centers to pay for transmission infrastructure, screening projects for grid impacts, ending tax breaks and giving communities more say. She has repeated the calls during her campaign. Investors and analysts believe a pause or added costs could slow new data center construction and, in turn, constrain AI computing capacity. They fear that a major Democratic win could strengthen the growing nationwide push for data center restrictions. Texas is home to data centers operated by Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, as well as AI campuses developed by Crusoe for customers including OpenAI, Oracle, Microsoft and Google. Several companies are expanding or building new Texas campuses. Democrats have won control of the U.S. Senate and are on the brink of taking the House in a widespread repudiation of Trump, according to the latest reporting by the Associated Press. Official certification of results comes weeks later. Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in, with cloud stocks dropping sharply overnight. Hyperscalers Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT), and Alphabet (GOOGL) fell 0.4% to 1% ahead of Wednesday, while Oracle (ORCL) fell sharply by 2.3%. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave (CRWV) and Iren Ltd. (IREN) dropped 3.3% and 4.3%, respectively, while Applied Digital (APLD) slid 3%. Among chipmakers, Intel (INTC) slid 0.7% while Nvidia (NVDA) was flat. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a cheeky post on X. Some commentators, however, said concerns about slowing data center buildout were overblown or already priced in by investors. “If companies ask for no subsidies, promise a ton of union jobs, and guarantee that water and electricity costs won't rise/plus add supply, data centers can be built under her governorship,” said "Key Context" newsletter author Tae Kim in an X post, referring to a proposed concessions on Hinojosa’s website. “Data centers will come under scrutiny but that fear has been adequately priced in at this point. Many Republicans campaigned on tighter permitting too,” Michael Sikand, a trader and founder of financial media company Our Future, said in an X post. According to trading firm Liquid, Iren and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) have substantial Texas exposure through projects such as Sweetwater and Helios, making the treatment of future expansion especially important. Nebius and Applied Digital have less direct exposure, with their disclosed core AI campuses outside Texas. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ for GOOGL and AMZN, ‘bullish’ for MSFT, and ‘bearish’ for META. The sentiment was ‘bearish’ for CRWV, APLD and IREN. “$CRWV results of the mid term will have little effect on tech stock long terms. Tech companies have survived administrations under both parties,” a trader said. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com.
